newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Court requires mutual recognition of military service.
newsitem.headline: Court requires mutual recognition of military service.

text.p: The European Court of Justice said on Wednesday if a member state stops the clock from running on education benefits during mandatory military service, it must recognize military service in all member states.
German law extends benefits for full-time education or vocational training to orphans until the age of 25, and extends that period to include military service or equivalent civil duties.

A Spanish national, whose father died while working in Germany, began receiving orphan benefits from the Rhine Province when he started his educational and vocational training. Germany later refused to take into account his military service period in Spain and to extend his benefits beyond his 25th birthday for the same period.

Although the court found treaty rights for the freedom of movement of workers require Germany to recognize military service carried out in other member states, in this case the applicant is not protected because Spain was not a member of the European Union when his father died. Consequently, the father did not have the status of "worker" under treaty article 48.

"The refusal to assimilate military service in another member state to military service completed in the state concerned is liable to result in nationals of other member states being unable to benefit from the right to extension" in violation of the freedom of movement for workers, the court said.
Reference for a preliminary ruling by the Bundessozialgericht pending before that court between

on the interpretation of articles 5, 48, 51 of the EC Treaty and article 7 of regulation (EEC) No 1612/68 of the Council of 15 October 1968 1612/68 on freedom of movement for workers within the Community (OJ, English Special Edition 1968 (II), p. 475)

Article 3(1) of Council regulation (EEC) No 1408/71 on the application of social security schemes to employed persons, to self-employed persons and to members of their families moving within the Community, as amended and updated by Council regulation No 2001/83, must be interpreted as meaning that where the legislation of a member state provides for extension of the right to orphan's benefit beyond the age of 25 for recipients of benefits whose training has been interrupted by their military service, that state is required to assimilate military service in another member state to military service under its own legislation.
